citation.title: Field Experiments and the Study of Voter Turnout
citation.venue: Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties

standing_assumptions:
The article (Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties 23(1):27–48, 2013; the staged edition carries the footer “This version has been corrected”, p. 27) is a review of field experiments on voter turnout. It has no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof, no displayed formula, no mathematical notation, no table and no figure; every statistical statement is made in words and the pooled estimates are given in running text. Printed page = PDF page + 24 (printed p. 27 is PDF p. 3). Everything quoted below was read from the page images.
(S1) Experiments. p. 28 (PDF p. 4): “An experiment is a study in which the units of observation are assigned at random with known probability to treatment and control conditions. Field experiments are randomized studies that take place in real-world settings.”
(S2) Potential outcomes. p. 30 (PDF p. 6): “First, random assignment is a procedure that ensures that the potential outcomes of those in the treatment group are, in expectation, the same as the potential outcomes in the control group.$^{2}$” Note 2, pp. 39–40 (PDF pp. 15–16): “2. The term “potential outcomes” refers to the outcomes that a subject would express depending on whether he or she receives the treatment. Untreated subjects express their untreated potential outcome, while treated subjects express their treated potential outcome. When treatments are administered at random, treatment is independent of subjects’ potential outcomes.”
(S3) Pooling method. p. 31 (PDF p. 7): “Given the sheer volume of studies, we summarize the results using meta-analysis rather than describing each study individually. Meta-analysis is a statistical method that pools the experiments in a given domain, weighting each study by the precision with which it estimates the treatment effect. This fixed effects weighting scheme means that smaller experiments tend to be accorded less weight than larger studies. The voter turnout literature is in many ways well-suited to meta-analysis insofar as the outcomes are measured along the same metric (percentage point increases in turnout), and the treatments within a given domain are relatively similar.$^{3}$” Note 3, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “3. In order to minimize variation in the nature of each treatment, we exclude from our meta-analysis compound treatments, such as a mixture of direct mail and phone calls, and discuss them below with regard to hypotheses about synergy and diminishing returns.” Note 4, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “4. We count experimental treatments at varying levels of aggregation, including averaging across multiple experiments in multiple geographic regions. In so doing, we underestimate the number of total treatments deployed.” The paper prints no formula for the weights, for the weighted average, for its variance or for the confidence interval, and it states no condition on the dependence between the estimates that are pooled.
(S4) Outcome scales. Mail, p. 31 (PDF p. 7): “In all, 147 distinct experimental treatments assessed the effects of direct mail, sometimes sending several mailings to a given recipient.$^{4}$ Using linear regression, we estimated the percentage-point increase in turnout per mailing.” Canvassing and live calls: the Complier average causal effect of (S5). Recorded calls, Note 5, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “5. Because studies of recorded calls have very high contact rates (which include messages left on answering machines), we consider the effect of assignment. To obtain a rough estimate of the CACE, divide the effect of assignment by 0.8.”
(S5) Noncompliance. p. 32 (PDF p. 8): “As we turn our attention to canvassing and phone calls, we confront a complication. Canvassers and callers sometimes fail to reach their intended targets. Experiments are unable to assess the effects of a treatment on the type of person that Angrist et al. (1996) dub “Never-takers,” those who would not be contacted if called or visited. Instead, experiments that fail to treat some of the members of the assigned treatment group are limited to estimating the average treatment effect among “Compliers,” those who would be contacted if visited or called. The average treatment effect for this subgroup is estimated by calculating the difference in turnout rates between those assigned to treatment and control and dividing this difference by the fraction of the assigned treatment group that actually receives the treatment (see Gerber & Green, 2012: chapter 5). For each canvassing and calling study in our meta-analysis, we use this formula to estimate the Complier average causal effect (CACE).”
(S6) Data. Note 1, p. 39 (PDF p. 15): “1. Data used for the meta-analyses reported in this article are available at http://isps.research.yale.edu/research.” The staged replication material (staged/code/yale-dataverse-ACAJSM-v2.0) is a CSV with one row per pooled estimate (an effect and its standard error) and a Stata program of ten calls of the form `metan <effect> <se> [if ...], label(namevar=title) fixed nograph`; no call takes a covariance between rows.
(S7) Audit notation, not in the paper (from the validators' derivations). For a pool of $J$ estimates: $d_j$ (as a random variable, $D_j$) is the $j$-th effect estimate in percentage points and $s_j$ its standard error; $w_j = 1/s_j^2$, $W = \sum_j w_j$, $a_j = w_j/W$; the pooled estimate is $\hat\theta = \sum_j a_j d_j$; $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of $(D_1,\dots,D_J)$ with $\Sigma_{jj} = s_j^2$. The validators reproduce every pooled estimate and interval printed on pp. 31–33, to the three printed decimals, as $\hat\theta \pm \Phi^{-1}(0.975)\sqrt{1/W}$ from the deposited rows.
Scope of the list. Two confirmed errors change the mathematics that is applied and are targets: P042-E001 (the variance behind every pooled interval omits the covariance between estimates that share a control group) and P042-E002 (the figure of Note 5 is not the declared fixed-effects average). The confirmed errors P042-N003, P042-N005, P042-N006, P042-N010 and P042-N011 are errors in the inputs of the pools (five estimates on the wrong scale, overlapping samples, an experiment entered twice and, in each of two pools, a row that the text says is excluded): the validators find the printed numbers to be the correct output of the declared calculation on the deposited rows, and their corrections replace empirical estimates by pooling different rows without changing any formula, identity or assumption, so they are findings about data and are not targets. P042-E003, P042-E004, P042-E005 and P042-N012 concern dataset metadata, the reference list and a citation and are not targets. Of the ten headline claims, P042-H2 to P042-H5 are empirical estimates and P042-H6 to P042-H10 are interpretive summaries; only P042-H1 contains mathematical statements (P042-T6).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Unnumbered statements: under random assignment the potential outcomes of the treatment and control groups are the same in expectation (p. 30 with Note 2), and the contact-rate formula for the Complier average causal effect (p. 32)
canonical_claim.location: p. 30 (PDF p. 6) with Note 2 on pp. 39–40 (PDF pp. 15–16); p. 32 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 30 (PDF p. 6)] “The use of a randomly allocated treatment has two important advantages. First, random assignment is a procedure that ensures that the potential outcomes of those in the treatment group are, in expectation, the same as the potential outcomes in the control group.$^{2}$ Comparability of treatment and control groups is no longer a matter of speculation.”
[Note 2, pp. 39–40 (PDF pp. 15–16)] “2. The term “potential outcomes” refers to the outcomes that a subject would express depending on whether he or she receives the treatment. Untreated subjects express their untreated potential outcome, while treated subjects express their treated potential outcome. When treatments are administered at random, treatment is independent of subjects’ potential outcomes.”
[p. 32 (PDF p. 8)] “As we turn our attention to canvassing and phone calls, we confront a complication. Canvassers and callers sometimes fail to reach their intended targets. Experiments are unable to assess the effects of a treatment on the type of person that Angrist et al. (1996) dub “Never-takers,” those who would not be contacted if called or visited. Instead, experiments that fail to treat some of the members of the assigned treatment group are limited to estimating the average treatment effect among “Compliers,” those who would be contacted if visited or called. The average treatment effect for this subgroup is estimated by calculating the difference in turnout rates between those assigned to treatment and control and dividing this difference by the fraction of the assigned treatment group that actually receives the treatment (see Gerber & Green, 2012: chapter 5). For each canvassing and calling study in our meta-analysis, we use this formula to estimate the Complier average causal effect (CACE).”
[Illustration, p. 32 (PDF p. 8)] “For example, the Michelson (2006) study found that canvassing increased turnout among young Latino voters from 7.0% to 9.4%. Given a contact rate of 50%, the estimated CACE is 4.8 percentage points.”
[Formal reading by the audit; the paper prints no formula and no notation.]
(a) [Same in expectation] $N \ge 2$ subjects with fixed potential outcomes $Y_i(0), Y_i(1)$ (turnout, in $\{0,1\}$; the claim holds for real values). The assignment $Z \in \{0,1\}^N$ is drawn by complete randomization with $m$ subjects assigned to treatment, $1 \le m \le N-1$ (every subset of size $m$ equally likely). Then for $t \in \{0,1\}$ $$E\Big[\frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_iY_i(t)\Big] = E\Big[\frac{1}{N-m}\sum_i (1-Z_i)Y_i(t)\Big] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i Y_i(t).$$ Consequently, with observed outcomes $Y_i = Y_i(Z_i)$, $E\big[\frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_iY_i - \frac{1}{N-m}\sum_i (1-Z_i)Y_i\big] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i [Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$.
(b) [Contact-rate formula] In addition each subject has a contact indicator $c_i \in \{0,1\}$: $c_i = 1$ for a Complier (‘would be contacted if visited or called’) and $c_i = 0$ for a Never-taker; a subject is contacted exactly when $Z_ic_i = 1$, so nobody assigned to control is contacted; and the observed outcome is $Y_i = Y_i(Z_ic_i)$, where $Y_i(1)$, $Y_i(0)$ are the potential outcomes with and without contact (assignment affects turnout only through the subject's own contact). Let $N_C = \sum_i c_i \ge 1$ and $\pi_C = N_C/N$. Define $\mathrm{ITT} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i [Y_i(c_i) - Y_i(0)]$ and $\mathrm{CACE} = \frac{1}{N_C}\sum_i c_i[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$. Then: (b1) $\mathrm{ITT} = \pi_C \cdot \mathrm{CACE}$; (b2) under the complete randomization of (a), $E[\bar Y_T - \bar Y_C] = \mathrm{ITT}$, where $\bar Y_T = \frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_iY_i$ and $\bar Y_C = \frac{1}{N-m}\sum_i (1-Z_i)Y_i$ are the turnout rates of those assigned to treatment and to control, and $E\big[\frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_ic_i\big] = \pi_C$, the expected fraction of the assigned treatment group that is contacted; (b3) hence $$\mathrm{CACE} = \frac{E[\bar Y_T - \bar Y_C]}{E\big[\frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_ic_i\big]}.$$ (b4) [The printed illustration] $(9.4 - 7.0)/0.50 = 4.8$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: an experiment (‘assigned at random with known probability to treatment and control conditions’, p. 28, standing assumption (S1)); potential outcomes (Note 2, quoted above); Never-takers and Compliers, and the estimator in words (p. 32, quoted above; the paper refers to Angrist et al. (1996) and Gerber & Green (2012, chapter 5), neither of which is staged). A further use of the formula, Note 5, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “To obtain a rough estimate of the CACE, divide the effect of assignment by 0.8.” The paper does not define ‘in expectation’, the assignment mechanism or the estimand formally, and it does not list the conditions of (b) (nobody in the control group is contacted; assignment affects turnout only through contact; no interference between subjects; a positive share of Compliers); they are those of the framework the paragraph sets up and cites. Standard meanings used in the reading: expectation over the random assignment with the potential outcomes held fixed; the Complier average causal effect is the average of $Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ over the Compliers; ‘the fraction of the assigned treatment group that actually receives the treatment’ is $\frac{1}{m}\sum_i Z_ic_i$.
canonical_claim.note: Verbal statements of an identity; the rendering is the audit's, and a fidelity check should treat it as a reading and not as the paper's formula. P042-H1 as a whole is a methodological claim (field experiments overcome the weaknesses of survey research); only the two statements above have exact mathematical content, and the article applies the second to every canvassing and live-call estimate. The paper says only ‘assigned at random with known probability’; the reading fixes complete randomization so that (a) and (b2) are exact (for any design with exactly $m$ treated and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = m/N$ for every $i$ the same proof by linearity applies). What is exact is the identity (b1)–(b3) between expectations; the estimator the paper describes, $(\bar Y_T - \bar Y_C)$ divided by the fraction contacted, is a ratio of two unbiased estimators and is not itself unbiased, and its consistency is an asymptotic statement that the paper does not make and that is not part of this target. Both fresh readers checked these passages: Opus reports that they held up against the standard results for one-sided noncompliance; Sol that they held up with the caveat that randomization alone does not supply the exclusion and no-interference conditions. That caveat is candidate P042-A001, which Sol's validation did not confirm (the formula is the standard estimator read in the framework the paragraph cites; class not_confirmed in ratings.json), so related_finding is null. No confirmed finding touches these statements. The other headline claims are empirical estimates (P042-H2 to P042-H5) or interpretive summaries (P042-H6 to P042-H10) and are not targets.
